facts.text: Sūtra Nexus is a free study desk for three open data files: 3,983 Aṣṭādhyāyī lines, 14 Māheśvara lines, and 75 Kashmir Śiva Sūtras. It is a learning project by a lifelong student and AI enthusiast moving toward AI omni-channel agents.
The start path has six steps. Progress marks stay in this browser. Nothing is uploaded.
Meaning field for every canon line in this app: meaning: not yet sourced from an open text. IAST from the Aṣṭādhyāyī file is script-converted, not yet human-checked.
A short plain-English line in this app is a learner's note (not a translation). It teaches how the app is organized. It is not a scholar's rendering of a sūtra.
sūtra: A short rule line. This app shows the source text and does not translate it.
IAST: A Latin transliteration scheme. Here it is script-converted unless a row says otherwise.
The rows in this app are written in Devanāgarī. English Wikipedia's Devanagari page, checked 2026-10-16, describes it in the short description as an Indic script used in the Indian subcontinent.

IAST is the Latin scheme used beside those rows. English Wikipedia's IAST page, checked the same day, calls it a transliteration scheme for Indic scripts. In the Aṣṭādhyāyī file the IAST was produced by a script and has not been checked by a person. The label is: script-converted, not yet human-checked.

English Wikipedia's Shiksha page, checked 2026-10-16, calls Śikṣā a Vedic-era study of phonetics and phonology, one of six Vedangas. Sthāna (place) and prayatna (effort) are the classroom names for phonetic charts. This app does not draw those charts, because no open phonetic edition was opened and recorded. Confirm before relying on any place-of-articulation table you bring from elsewhere.
What you can trust here is the 14-line sound list in the data file, printed as the file records it.
Devanāgarī: The script of the source lines in these files.
sthāna: A traditional name for place of articulation. Not charted here. Confirm before relying.
prayatna: A traditional name for articulatory effort. Not charted here. Confirm before relying.

The file data/maheshvara.json holds 14 lines. English Wikipedia's Shiva Sutras article, checked 2026-10-16, uses the short description "14 verses organizing the phonemes of Sanskrit" and tells readers that the Kashmir text is a different article. That Wikipedia page also says it needs more citations, so this app treats the file, not the article, as the list.

Each line has sounds and a final marker. A pratyāhāra in this app is a computed set: start at a sound, walk forward, and stop at a chosen marker line. The marker itself is not kept. This is an operation on the file, not a translation.
The self-test checks ac, ik, yaṇ, śar, ak, ec, hal (33 sounds), and al (42 sounds).
The IAST strings in that file are script-converted, not yet human-checked. The Devanāgarī and the sounds arrays are what the builder uses.
pratyāhāra: In this app, a set computed from a start sound and a marker line.
it marker: The final marker on a line. The builder does not keep it in the set.
ac: The computed set: a i u ṛ ḷ e o ai au.
English Wikipedia's Sandhi page, checked 2026-10-16, uses the short description "type of sound change at morpheme or syllable boundaries." This app uses that as the plain name of the topic.

A sandhi rule in the Aṣṭādhyāyī tradition is often taught as naming a set of sounds with a pratyāhāra, then stating what happens when those sounds meet. This app can show the set, because the set is computed from the 14 lines. It cannot show the operation of a particular rule, because the English of that rule is not yet sourced from an open text.
There is no sample join such as a textbook word pair on this page. Adding one would be writing a result this project has not cited.
Learner's note (not a translation): when you are ready to study a real rule, open a sourced edition, find the pratyāhāra it names, and check that set in the builder. Confirm before relying.
sandhi: Sound change where pieces meet, per the Wikipedia short description cited here.
set: The sounds a pratyāhāra names in this app's computation.
The file holds 3,983 rows. English Wikipedia's Aṣṭādhyāyī page, checked 2026-10-16, also says 3,983 sūtras in eight chapters, each subdivided into four pādas.
Chapter counts in this file are 351, 268, 631, 635, 555, 736, 438, 369. They sum to 3,983.

The file's type letters are AD 64, AT 67, P 23, S 200, V 3629. The file meta glosses S as saṃjñā, P as paribhāṣā, and V as vidhi. It does not gloss AT or AD. This app does not expand those two letters. Confirm before relying.

Wikipedia's list of ancillary types, on the page checked the same day, names paribhāṣā as metarules, adhikāra as headings, atideśa as extension rules, niyama as restrictive rules, and pratiṣedha and niṣedha as negation rules, beside vidhi as the operational rules. This app does not assert that the file's AT or AD letters are those words.
Every row's meaning is not yet sourced from an open text.
adhyāya: A chapter. The file numbers them 1 through 8.
pāda: A section of a chapter. Wikipedia's page says four per chapter.
saṃjñā: The file meta's gloss for type letter S. Not a translation of a sūtra.
vidhi: The file meta's gloss for type letter V, and Wikipedia's name for an operational rule.
3489 of the 3,983 rows have a non-empty anuvritti array. The other rows have an empty array. That is a count, not a theory.

Learner's note (not a translation): classrooms use anuvṛtti for words that carry forward from an earlier line so the later line can stay short. This app shows the strings the file stored. It does not decide whether a string was carried correctly.
On 1.1.3 the Devanāgarī is इको गुणवृद्धी. The file's IAST is iko guṇavṛddhī and is script-converted, not yet human-checked. The anuvritti field lists: वृद्धिः, गुणः.
The padaccheda field on that row is also stored in the file. It is shown as file data, not as this project's analysis. Meaning: not yet sourced from an open text.
anuvṛtti: The classroom name for words understood from earlier lines. The file field is anuvritti.
padaccheda: The file's word-split field. Not re-analyzed here.

Learner's note (not a translation): dhātu is the classroom name for a verb root, and a pada is a finished word. People also meet tiṅ (verb endings) and sup (nominal endings) as names of ending sets. This page does not quote a sūtra that defines them, because that would be a translation.

The Aṣṭādhyāyī data file has no dhātu inventory. The repository README of ashtadhyayi-com/data, opened 2026-10-16, mentions dhātu forms as data the website edits, but those forms are not in the three JSON files shipped here.
So this room teaches the gap. You can learn the words as labels. You cannot look up a root's forms in this app yet.
Confirm before relying on any root list you remember from a class until it is tied to an opened edition.
dhātu: Classroom name for a verb root. No inventory in this app. Confirm before relying.
pada: Classroom name for a finished word.
tiṅ: Classroom name for a set of verb endings. Not quoted from a sūtra here.
sup: Classroom name for a set of nominal endings. Not quoted from a sūtra here.

This page is not the 14 Māheśvara lines. English Wikipedia's Shiva Sutras of Vasugupta page, checked 2026-10-16, calls that work a collection of aphorisms from Kashmir Shaivism in its short description.

The file has 75 rows. Its meta note says this recension counts 20+10+45=75, and that the common Kṣemarāja recension counts 22+10+45, then the note trails off. Which lines differ is unknown beyond that note. Confirm before relying.

The file says its IAST comes from the GRETIL source and that the Devanāgarī was machine-converted and is unverified. The GRETIL page, opened 2026-10-16, distributes the e-text under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Those non-commercial and share-alike terms stay with the e-text. Nothing here is sold.
No English meaning is included. A translation was not confirmed as open.
unmeṣa: The file groups lines into sections numbered on each row. This app does not translate the word.
recension: A version of a text. This file describes its own count and trails off on the other.

English Wikipedia's Pāṇini article, checked 2026-10-16, treats the dates as disputed. It reports that George Cardona (1997) says the available evidence strongly supports a date no earlier than 400 BCE, and that earlier dates rely on interpretations that are not probative.
The same article reports that Oskar von Hinüber (1989) and Harry Falk (1993) place Pāṇini in the mid-4th century BCE. This app does not choose between those reports.
The article mentions Kātyāyana and Patañjali inside that dating discussion. This page does not assign either of them a century, because that sentence was not the one copied into the notes.
All of these years are approximate scholarly estimates as reported by that encyclopedia page. Confirm before relying. Nothing here is a primary source.
approximate: The article's dates are scholarly estimates. This app marks them that way.
Each drawing has three files: an SVG, a PNG of that SVG, and a standalone HTML page. The disclaimer is inside all three.
A moving dot means reading order. If you asked the browser to reduce motion, the dot is hidden and the boxes stay.
Counts on a chart are from the JSON files. A mind map is a map of this app, not a claim about history.
diagram: A drawing with a title, a caption, and a source line.
A bar is a count of rows in a file in this repository. It is not a survey and not a popularity rank.
Chapter bars add up to 3,983. The type-letter bars use the letters stored on each row.
AT and AD stay unexpanded. The file meta glosses S, P, and V only.
bar: A count from a JSON file, named in the caption.
A link on this page was opened in October 2026 and the licence line is what that page said then.
Wikipedia text is CC BY-SA. The GRETIL e-text page states CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The data README asks for credit and states no SPDX.
Vasu's English was not confirmed, so no words from it appear. Confirm before relying on any meaning you add later.
source: A page that was opened, with the licence written down.
Games check a number or a gloss that this app already states. They do not score you on a translation.
Flashcards use a simple ladder on this device: again is about a minute, then a day, three days, and seven.
Interview answers are generic and cited. They are not a résumé and not someone's job story.
pratyāhāra: A set computed from a start sound and a marker line.
The 1-minute clip, the 10-minute trailer, and the 1-hour walk are scripts you read. There is no video file and no Sanskrit recording.
Voice in the guide is off until you turn it on. A browser voice may mispronounce Sanskrit. It is a reading aid.
The one-hour course repeats sentences already written in the rooms and then asks a checkpoint.
scripted read: Text you read on the page. Not an audio file.
This is a free learning project by a lifelong student and AI enthusiast moving toward AI omni-channel agents.
Nothing here is sold. Corrections go through the contact form. There is no email address on this site.
The 3D wheel loads only if you ask, on a wide screen, with motion allowed. Phones keep the still poster.
contact form: The link in the disclaimer. Not an email address.
Code libraries in vendor/ are MIT or ISC. They are not loaded on the first screen except where a page says so.
Simple Icons 13.21.0 are CC0. Noto Sans Devanagari is OFL 1.1. The two 3D models are original and marked CC0.
The Webex Lab kit was adapted from commit 7631b317cbf2cad236403df960b5d5fac353a6de. Webex and Cisco product copy is not used.
vendor: A library file kept in this repository, with its licence named.
Each study room ends with a glossary, sister topics, a bridge, and a later hook. This page gathers the maps.
A bridge is a learner's note. It is not a quotation from Pāṇini and not a claim that the tradition described software.
No NLP paper is cited here. Confirm before relying if you attach one.
bridge: A learner's analogy, labeled, and not a translation.
Every drawing is an SVG, a PNG, and an HTML page. Every 3D model is a GLB, a PNG poster, and a credits file.
Cheat sheets are PDF, HTML, and PNG. Templates are DOCX, PDF, and HTML. Flashcards are PDF, JSON, and HTML.
There is one optional zip, sutra-nexus-all.zip. It is the only archive. The same files are also listed one by one.
optional zip: One archive that repeats the individual files. You can skip it.
A glossary line is the wording used in this app. If it is not a quotation, it is a learner's note.
Sthāna and prayatna are named and then marked as not charted. Confirm before relying on a chart from somewhere else.
The same term can appear on the room that introduced it. This table points back there.
glossary: A short note for a term used in these rooms.

steps.title: Sūtra Nexus
steps.text: Sūtra Nexus is a free study desk for three open data files: 3,983 Aṣṭādhyāyī lines, 14 Māheśvara lines, and 75 Kashmir Śiva Sūtras. It is a learning project by a lifelong student and AI enthusiast moving toward AI omni-channel agents.

steps.title: Foundations
steps.text: The rows in this app are written in Devanāgarī. English Wikipedia's Devanagari page, checked 2026-10-16, describes it in the short description as an Indic script used in the Indian subcontinent.

steps.title: Māheśvara lines and pratyāhāra
steps.text: The file data/maheshvara.json holds 14 lines. English Wikipedia's Shiva Sutras article, checked 2026-10-16, uses the short description "14 verses organizing the phonemes of Sanskrit" and tells readers that the Kashmir text is a different article. That Wikipedia page also says it needs more citations, so this app treats the file, not the article, as the list.

steps.title: Sandhi basics
steps.text: English Wikipedia's Sandhi page, checked 2026-10-16, uses the short description "type of sound change at morpheme or syllable boundaries." This app uses that as the plain name of the topic.

steps.title: Aṣṭādhyāyī structure
steps.text: The file holds 3,983 rows. English Wikipedia's Aṣṭādhyāyī page, checked 2026-10-16, also says 3,983 sūtras in eight chapters, each subdivided into four pādas.

steps.title: Anuvṛtti
steps.text: 3489 of the 3,983 rows have a non-empty anuvritti array. The other rows have an empty array. That is a count, not a theory.

steps.title: Dhātu and pada basics
steps.text: Learner's note (not a translation): dhātu is the classroom name for a verb root, and a pada is a finished word. People also meet tiṅ (verb endings) and sup (nominal endings) as names of ending sets. This page does not quote a sūtra that defines them, because that would be a translation.

steps.title: Śiva Sūtras, Kashmir text
steps.text: This page is not the 14 Māheśvara lines. English Wikipedia's Shiva Sutras of Vasugupta page, checked 2026-10-16, calls that work a collection of aphorisms from Kashmir Shaivism in its short description.

steps.title: History and timeline
steps.text: English Wikipedia's Pāṇini article, checked 2026-10-16, treats the dates as disputed. It reports that George Cardona (1997) says the available evidence strongly supports a date no earlier than 400 BCE, and that earlier dates rely on interpretations that are not probative.

steps.title: Diagrams
steps.text: Each drawing has three files: an SVG, a PNG of that SVG, and a standalone HTML page. The disclaimer is inside all three.

steps.title: Charts
steps.text: A bar is a count of rows in a file in this repository. It is not a survey and not a popularity rank.

steps.title: Resources
steps.text: A link on this page was opened in October 2026 and the licence line is what that page said then.

steps.title: Play
steps.text: Games check a number or a gloss that this app already states. They do not score you on a translation.

steps.title: Listen
steps.text: The 1-minute clip, the 10-minute trailer, and the 1-hour walk are scripts you read. There is no video file and no Sanskrit recording.

steps.title: About
steps.text: This is a free learning project by a lifelong student and AI enthusiast moving toward AI omni-channel agents.

steps.text: Code libraries in vendor/ are MIT or ISC. They are not loaded on the first screen except where a page says so.

steps.title: Ecosystem
steps.text: Each study room ends with a glossary, sister topics, a bridge, and a later hook. This page gathers the maps.

steps.title: Downloads
steps.text: Every drawing is an SVG, a PNG, and an HTML page. Every 3D model is a GLB, a PNG poster, and a credits file.

steps.text: A glossary line is the wording used in this app. If it is not a quotation, it is a learner's note.

glossary.defn: A short rule line. This app shows the source text and does not translate it.
A Latin transliteration scheme. Here it is script-converted unless a row says otherwise.
The script of the source lines in these files.
A traditional name for place of articulation. Not charted here. Confirm before relying.
A traditional name for articulatory effort. Not charted here. Confirm before relying.
In this app, a set computed from a start sound and a marker line.
The final marker on a line. The builder does not keep it in the set.
The computed set: a i u ṛ ḷ e o ai au.
Sound change where pieces meet, per the Wikipedia short description cited here.
The sounds a pratyāhāra names in this app's computation.
A chapter. The file numbers them 1 through 8.
A section of a chapter. Wikipedia's page says four per chapter.
The file meta's gloss for type letter S. Not a translation of a sūtra.
The file meta's gloss for type letter V, and Wikipedia's name for an operational rule.
The classroom name for words understood from earlier lines. The file field is anuvritti.
The file's word-split field. Not re-analyzed here.
Classroom name for a verb root. No inventory in this app. Confirm before relying.
Classroom name for a finished word.
Classroom name for a set of verb endings. Not quoted from a sūtra here.
Classroom name for a set of nominal endings. Not quoted from a sūtra here.
The file groups lines into sections numbered on each row. This app does not translate the word.
A version of a text. This file describes its own count and trails off on the other.
The article's dates are scholarly estimates. This app marks them that way.
A drawing with a title, a caption, and a source line.
A count from a JSON file, named in the caption.
A page that was opened, with the licence written down.
A set computed from a start sound and a marker line.
Text you read on the page. Not an audio file.
The link in the disclaimer. Not an email address.
A library file kept in this repository, with its licence named.
A learner's analogy, labeled, and not a translation.
One archive that repeats the individual files. You can skip it.
A short note for a term used in these rooms.
